title: The Economics of the Medieval Book
body:
Before paper reached northern Europe, every book was written on the skins of animals, and this single fact governed what medieval libraries could contain. A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep or calves, so that the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase. Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

The preparation of the skins was itself protracted. After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly. The two sides were never quite alike. The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering. Nothing about this labor could be hurried, and a failure at any stage ruined material that had taken a year of grazing to produce. Scribes accordingly treated the surface with a respect that modern readers, accustomed to abundant paper, may find difficult to imagine.

One consequence was that parchment was rarely discarded. A text that had lost its audience could be scraped a second time and written over, and the recycled sheet, known as a palimpsest, carried the faint traces of whatever it had previously borne. Scholars have recovered lost works of antiquity from beneath later devotional texts, and the accident that preserved them was economic rather than scholarly: a monastery short of skins reused what it judged obsolete. What survives from the ancient world was thus filtered not only by taste but by the price of a sheep.

The arrival of paper altered this arithmetic decisively. Manufactured from rags rather than livestock, paper could be produced in quantity by artisans who owned no land, and its cost fell as mills multiplied along the rivers of Italy and Germany. Printing, when it came, is often credited with the sudden abundance of books in the fifteenth century, yet a press without cheap sheets to feed it would have changed little. The two innovations are properly understood as a single development, in which a new method of duplication became consequential only because a new material had already made the page expendable. Skin did not vanish overnight. Charters and other documents intended to outlast their makers were still drawn on parchment long after paper had captured the ordinary book, a preference that reveals what each material was thought to promise.

questions.question: According to paragraph 1, why did book-producing monasteries need to be landholders?

choices.A: Because church law required monasteries to farm the land they occupied
choices.B: Because the animals whose skins became pages had to be raised and grazed
choices.C: Because scribes were recruited from the families of neighboring tenants
choices.D: Because libraries had to be housed in buildings large enough to store hides

questions.explanation: 第1段落に "the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase. Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first" とあり、羊や子牛の群れを飼うための土地が必要だったことが理由である。A、C、Dはいずれも本文に記述がない。

questions.question: The word "protracted" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: 直後に工程が段階的に描かれ、"Nothing about this labor could be hurried" と急げないことが明言されている。したがって protracted は時間的な長さを指し、C の lengthy が最も近い。A の expensive は第1段落の論点であって、この文が述べているのは所要時間である。

questions.question: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the ancient texts that survive today?

choices.A: They were copied more often than the texts that were lost
choices.B: They were valued more highly by medieval scholars than other works
choices.C: They were written on higher-quality parchment than the texts that vanished
choices.D: Their survival depended partly on circumstances unrelated to their merit

questions.explanation: 本文は "the accident that preserved them was economic rather than scholarly" と述べ、末尾で "filtered not only by taste but by the price of a sheep" と結んでいる。つまり残存は作品の価値だけで決まったのではない。BとCは本文が否定する「学術的・質的な理由」であり、Aは書写回数に関する記述が本文にない。

questions.question: The word "it" in paragraph 3 ("whatever it had previously borne") refers to

choices.B: the text that had lost its audience

questions.explanation: 当該部分は "the recycled sheet, known as a palimpsest, carried the faint traces of whatever it had previously borne" であり、以前に文字を担っていたのは再利用されたその紙葉自体である。Bの失われた読者を持つテキストは紙葉が担っていた内容の側であって、担い手ではない。

questions.question: Why does the author state that "a press without cheap sheets to feed it would have changed little"?

choices.A: To argue that printing was invented later than most historians believe
choices.B: To qualify the common view that printing alone produced the abundance of books
choices.C: To suggest that early presses were mechanically unreliable
choices.D: To explain why paper mills were built beside rivers

questions.explanation: この文は直前の "Printing... is often credited with the sudden abundance of books" を yet で受けており、印刷術のみを原因とする通説に留保を付ける役割を担う。続く一文が両者を "a single development" と位置づけることからも、目的は通説の修正である。Aの発明年代やCの機械的信頼性は論じられていない。

governed.etymology: ラテン語 gubernare(舵を取る) < ギリシャ語 kybernan → govern + -ed
governed.usage_in_passage: 冒頭の "this single fact governed what medieval libraries could contain" が本文の主張を一文で提示する。材料という物質的条件が知的な事柄を左右したという逆説を導入する。
governed.context_sentence: Before paper reached northern Europe, every book was written on the skins of animals, and this single fact governed what medieval libraries could contain.

medieval.etymology: ラテン語 medium(中間の) + aevum(時代) → 「中世の」
medieval.usage_in_passage: 議論の時代を限定し、紙が普及する以前という前提を設定する。
medieval.context_sentence: Before paper reached northern Europe, every book was written on the skins of animals, and this single fact governed what medieval libraries could contain.

consume.etymology: ラテン語 con-(すっかり) + sumere(取る) → 「使い尽くす」
consume.usage_in_passage: "A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep" で、本を作ることが家畜を消尽する行為であることを直截に示す。
consume.context_sentence: A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep or calves, so that the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase.

hundred.etymology: 古英語 hundred。ゲルマン系の数詞
hundred.usage_in_passage: "two hundred sheep or calves" という具体的な数字が、抽象的な「高価だった」という説明よりも強く規模を伝える。
hundred.context_sentence: A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep or calves, so that the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase.

sheep.etymology: 古英語 scēap。ゲルマン系で、単複同形
sheep.usage_in_passage: 第1段落で材料の供給源として登場し、最終段落の "the price of a sheep" で古典文献の残存を左右した要因として回収される。
sheep.context_sentence: A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep or calves, so that the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase.

calves.etymology: 古英語 cealf(子牛)の複数形。ゲルマン系
calves.usage_in_passage: 羊と並ぶ皮の供給源として挙げられ、上質の犢皮紙(ヴェラム)が子牛から作られたことを示唆する。
calves.context_sentence: A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep or calves, so that the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase.

herd.etymology: 古英語 heord(群れ)。ゲルマン系
herd.usage_in_passage: "the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase" が本文の中心的な比喩。本の原価が買い物ではなく畜産であったことを示す。
herd.context_sentence: A large volume might consume the hides of two hundred sheep or calves, so that the raw material alone represented a herd rather than a purchase.

monasteries.etymology: ギリシャ語 monos(一人) → monastērion + -es
monasteries.usage_in_passage: 書物生産の担い手として、また第3段落では羊皮紙を再利用する経済主体として現れる。
monasteries.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

landholders.etymology: land + hold + -er + -s。ゲルマン系の複合語
landholders.usage_in_passage: "had to be landholders first and scholars second" という語順自体が主張を運ぶ。学問より先に土地が要るという優先順位が本文の逆説を要約している。
landholders.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

scholars.etymology: 後期ラテン語 scholaris < ギリシャ語 skholē(余暇、学校) + -s
scholars.usage_in_passage: landholders と対置され、修道院の性格が知的というより経済的であったことを際立たせる。
scholars.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

reflected.etymology: ラテン語 re-(戻って) + flectere(曲げる) → 「反映する」
reflected.definition: 映し出した、表していた。
reflected.usage_in_passage: "the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures" で、蔵書量が牧草地の広さの関数であったことを示す。
reflected.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

extent.etymology: ラテン語 ex-(外に) + tendere(伸ばす) → extend の名詞形
extent.usage_in_passage: 牧草地の面積を指し、直後の "the learning of the monks" と並置されることで、物質と知性が同等に蔵書を規定したことを示す。
extent.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

pastures.etymology: ラテン語 pascere(牧草を食べさせる) → pastura + -s
pastures.usage_in_passage: 図書館の規模を決める物理的資源として、学識と並べて提示される。
pastures.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

attached.etymology: 古フランス語 estachier(杭で留める)。ゲルマン語 stake と同系
attached.usage_in_passage: "the pastures attached to it" が、修道院と土地が制度上一体であったことを示す。
attached.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

faithfully.etymology: ラテン語 fides(信頼) → faith + -ful + -ly
faithfully.usage_in_passage: "as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks" で、二つの対応関係が同程度に強いことを述べ、物質的条件を学識と同格に置く。
faithfully.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

monks.etymology: ギリシャ語 monakhos(独りで暮らす者) → 古英語 munuc + -s
monks.usage_in_passage: "the learning of the monks" が、通常なら蔵書量の説明として第一に挙がる要因であり、本文はそれを土地と並列に格下げしている。
monks.context_sentence: Monasteries that produced books therefore had to be landholders first and scholars second, and the size of a collection reflected the extent of the pastures attached to it as faithfully as it reflected the learning of the monks.

preparation.etymology: ラテン語 prae-(前もって) + parare(整える) + -ation
preparation.usage_in_passage: 第2段落の主題語。"The preparation of the skins was itself protracted" が、材料費だけでなく加工の時間も制約であったことを示す。
preparation.context_sentence: The preparation of the skins was itself protracted.

protracted.etymology: ラテン語 pro-(前へ) + trahere(引く) → 「引き延ばされた」
protracted.definition: 長引いた、時間のかかる。
protracted.usage_in_passage: 語彙問題の対象語。直後に工程が順を追って描かれ、"Nothing about this labor could be hurried" が語義の手がかりとなる。
protracted.context_sentence: The preparation of the skins was itself protracted.

loosened.etymology: 古ノルド語 lauss(緩い) → loose + -en + -ed。ゲルマン系
loosened.definition: 緩めた、剥がれやすくした。
loosened.usage_in_passage: "After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime" が加工の第一段階を示し、石灰が毛を抜くために使われたことを説明する。
loosened.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

lime.etymology: 古英語 lim(粘着物)。ゲルマン系
lime.usage_in_passage: 毛を緩めるための薬剤として登場する。強アルカリの性質が皮を傷めずに毛だけを外す働きをする。
lime.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

stretched.etymology: 古英語 streccan(伸ばす)。ゲルマン系
stretched.usage_in_passage: "the hide was stretched on a frame" が、平滑な面を得るための張力処理を示し、次の scraped と対になる。
stretched.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

scraped.etymology: 古ノルド語 skrapa(こする)。ゲルマン系
scraped.usage_in_passage: 第2段落では皮を薄くする工程として、第3段落では "scraped a second time" として文字を消す工程として再登場し、同じ動作が製造と再利用の両方を担うことを示す。
scraped.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

repeatedly.etymology: ラテン語 re-(再び) + petere(求める) → repeat + -ed + -ly
repeatedly.usage_in_passage: 一度では済まない作業量を示し、protracted の語義を具体的に裏づける。
repeatedly.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

dried.etymology: 古英語 dryge(乾いた) → dry + -ed。ゲルマン系
dried.usage_in_passage: "while it dried under tension" で、乾燥と張力が同時に働くことが平滑な面を生むという工程の要点を示す。
dried.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

tension.etymology: ラテン語 tendere(張る) → tensio + -on
tension.usage_in_passage: 乾燥中に皮を張り続けることが、縮みや歪みを防ぐ鍵であったことを示す。
tension.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

yielded.etymology: 古英語 gieldan(支払う、産出する)。ゲルマン系
yielded.usage_in_passage: "a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly" で、相反する二つの要件を同時に満たす必要を示す。
yielded.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

folded.etymology: 古英語 fealdan(折る)。ゲルマン系
folded.usage_in_passage: sewn とともに、羊皮紙が単なる書写面ではなく製本に耐える素材でなければならなかったことを示す。
folded.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

sewn.etymology: 古英語 siwian(縫う)の過去分詞。ゲルマン系
sewn.usage_in_passage: 折丁を綴じる製本工程を指し、紙葉に求められる強度の理由を与える。
sewn.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

thin.etymology: 古英語 þynne(薄い)。ゲルマン系
thin.usage_in_passage: strong と対置され、"strong enough... yet thin enough" という譲歩構文が加工の難しさを表現する。
thin.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

cleanly.etymology: 古英語 clǣne(清潔な) → clean + -ly。ゲルマン系
cleanly.usage_in_passage: "thin enough to take ink cleanly" で、厚すぎるとインクが乗らないという実務上の要件を示す。
cleanly.context_sentence: After the hair was loosened in a bath of lime, the hide was stretched on a frame and scraped repeatedly while it dried under tension, a process that yielded a sheet strong enough to be folded and sewn yet thin enough to take ink cleanly.

alike.etymology: 古英語 gelīc(似た) → a- + like。ゲルマン系
alike.usage_in_passage: "The two sides were never quite alike" が短い一文で段落の焦点を転換し、表裏の差という新しい論点を導入する。
alike.context_sentence: The two sides were never quite alike.

borne.etymology: 古英語 beran(運ぶ、担う)の過去分詞。ゲルマン系
borne.definition: 担っていた、備えていた。
borne.usage_in_passage: 第2段落では "The face that had borne hair" として毛のあった面を、第3段落では "whatever it had previously borne" として以前の文字を指し、同じ語が物理面と内容の両方を担う。
borne.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

darker.etymology: 古英語 deorc(暗い) → dark + 比較級 -er。ゲルマン系
darker.usage_in_passage: coarser と並んで毛side の特徴を述べ、写字生が配慮せざるを得なかった差異を具体化する。
darker.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

coarser.etymology: 古英語 coarse(粗い) + 比較級 -er
coarser.usage_in_passage: darker と対になり、表裏の差が視覚と触覚の両面に及ぶことを示す。
coarser.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

lain.etymology: 古英語 licgan(横たわる)の過去分詞。ゲルマン系
lain.definition: 接していた、面していた。
lain.usage_in_passage: "the face that had lain against the flesh" で、肉に接していた側を指し、毛側との対比を完成させる。
lain.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

flesh.etymology: 古英語 flǣsc(肉)。ゲルマン系
flesh.usage_in_passage: 皮の内側を指す専門的な用法で、hair side と対をなす製本学の用語である。
flesh.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

scribes.etymology: ラテン語 scribere(書く) → scriba + -s
scribes.usage_in_passage: 第2段落で表裏を揃える工夫の主体として、また材料への敬意を示す主体として登場する。
scribes.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

arranged.etymology: 古フランス語 arengier(列に並べる) < a- + rank
arranged.usage_in_passage: "scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like" が、材料の欠点を編集で補う工夫を示す。
arranged.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

invisible.etymology: ラテン語 in-(否定) + videre(見る) + -ible
invisible.definition: 目に見えない、気づかれない。
invisible.usage_in_passage: obvious と対置され、この工夫が読者には意識されないまま機能していたことを示す。
invisible.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

obvious.etymology: ラテン語 ob-(前に) + via(道) → 「道の前にある」
obvious.usage_in_passage: invisible と対をなし、同じ事実が観察者の知識次第で見えたり見えなかったりすることを示す。
obvious.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

examines.etymology: ラテン語 examinare(秤で量る) < examen(秤の針)
examines.usage_in_passage: "anyone who examines the order of a gathering" が、専門的な観察によってのみ現れる証拠であることを示す。
examines.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

gathering.etymology: 古英語 gaderian(集める) → gather + -ing。ゲルマン系
gathering.definition: 折丁。数枚の紙葉を折り重ねた製本の単位。
gathering.usage_in_passage: 写本学の用語として使われ、表裏を揃える工夫が製本単位ごとに行われたことを示す。
gathering.context_sentence: The face that had borne hair stayed slightly darker and coarser than the face that had lain against the flesh, and scribes arranged the folded leaves so that like met like across each opening, an accommodation invisible to most readers but obvious to anyone who examines the order of a gathering.

hurried.etymology: 中英語 horyen(急がせる)。ゲルマン系 + -ed
hurried.usage_in_passage: "Nothing about this labor could be hurried" が protracted を言い換え、時間が短縮不能な制約であることを確認する。
hurried.context_sentence: Nothing about this labor could be hurried, and a failure at any stage ruined material that had taken a year of grazing to produce.

ruined.etymology: ラテン語 ruere(崩れ落ちる) → ruina + -ed
ruined.usage_in_passage: "a failure at any stage ruined material that had taken a year of grazing" が、失敗の代償を時間の単位で測り直し、第1段落の経済的主張と結びつける。
